annotations.text:
Pilot consent: one decision, whole category, no timer.
Access runs until the shopper disconnects. The set they allow is fixed by the brand's own categories, saved at signup — Essenza sells fragrance, so fragrance is all it can ask for.

Cross-brand products never leave Hallie by name.
A brand reads the notes and ingredients of what a shopper owns, not whose it is. Its own products it sees in full — name, purchase, rating, outcome.
What the brand shows back is the product of the deal: a ranked catalog with plain-language reasons, and a standing reminder that the shopper can cut it off.

The first dashboard only has to answer five questions: how many connected, what they want, what we recommended, whether it converted, and what the catalog is missing.
Everything here maps to one of those.

Later phases. Field-level consent, durations and expiry, and the permissions ledger all extend the pilot's grant record rather than replacing it — which is why the pilot writes purpose and scope on every grant even though it only offers one scope and no timer.
